issues.legal_issue: A party’s later failure to make payments promised under a family settlement does not make the settlement conditional or entitle the other party to rescind it when the agreement records that the transfer of rights has already occurred.
material_facts: The agreements recorded that the family members had relinquished or assigned their interests in the disputed properties, while the other party’s payment obligations were to be performed in the future.
The agreements’ references to the transfers being subject to payment did not make payment a precondition to the transfers.
The recipients sought payment after the specified dates had passed and did not initially treat timely payment as essential to the agreements.
issues.conclusion: The agreements were not conditional on payment, and a payment default did not give the recipients a right to rescind them; time was not treated by the parties as essential.
issues.legal_principle: The agreements must be construed as a whole: language about payment does not create a condition precedent where the agreements otherwise record that rights have already vested or been transferred. In that context, the payment terms impose a personal obligation, and breach gives a claim for payment rather than a right to rescind the settlement.

rule.if: challenge_to_compromise_decree and agreement_records_completed_transfer and payment_due_in_future and parties_did_not_treat_time_as_essential

predicates.challenge_to_compromise_decree: A party to a compromise decree seeks to set it aside because promised payment was not made.
predicates.agreement_records_completed_transfer: The settlement agreement records that the transfer or relinquishment of the relevant rights has already taken place or takes effect upon execution.
predicates.payment_due_in_future: The agreement requires the recipient of the rights to make payment after the transfer is recorded.
predicates.parties_did_not_treat_time_as_essential: The parties’ conduct shows that they sought payment after the stated payment dates rather than treating those dates as essential to the agreement.

issues.definition: When a party challenges a compromise decree after a recorded transfer and the parties treated payment as a future obligation rather than an essential condition, payment default does not entitle that party to rescind the settlement.

issues.legal_issue: A compromise decree may comply with the requirement for a written, signed compromise even when the court records separate agreements at different stages and later decrees the suits after all parties have settled.
material_facts: The relevant parties filed written applications setting out their respective agreements and supported them with affidavits affirming the facts.
The court first recorded the separate agreements while disputes with other parties remained unresolved, and later passed a decree after the remaining parties had settled their differences.
Each agreement was signed by the parties to that agreement; the appellants had already signed their own agreements and submitted affidavits supporting them.
The court recorded statements from the assignee who signed the final agreement and from representatives of the other heirs.
issues.conclusion: The procedure complied with Order XXIII Rule 3; the court was not required to record the appellants’ statements again or to obtain their signatures on the other parties’ separate agreement.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXIII Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires the court to be satisfied that the suit has been adjusted by a lawful written agreement signed by the parties, to record that agreement, and to pass a decree in accordance with it. Satisfaction may be presumed unless the contrary is shown. The staged recording of agreements is permissible where the settlement of all parties is completed before the final decree. Ajad Singh v. Chatra was distinguishable because there was no proceeding under Order XXIII Rule 3 and the compromise was not recorded through the procedure required by that rule.

rule.if: compromise_decree_proceeding and written_agreements_signed_by_relevant_parties and supporting_affidavits_on_record and all_parties_settled_before_final_decree

predicates.compromise_decree_proceeding: The court is asked to record a settlement and dispose of pending suits by compromise decree.
predicates.written_agreements_signed_by_relevant_pa: The parties to each separate settlement signed that written agreement.
predicates.supporting_affidavits_on_record: The applicants filed affidavits affirming the facts and supporting the compromise applications.
predicates.all_parties_settled_before_final_decree: The court passed the final decree only after the remaining parties to the suits had settled their disputes.

issues.definition: In a compromise-decree proceeding, signed written agreements supported by affidavits may be recorded in stages and support a final decree when all parties have settled before that decree.

issues.legal_issue: A family composition deed incorporated into a court decree does not require registration where it rearranges family interests and a provision concerning property outside the suits merely clarifies an earlier transaction.
material_facts: The agreements settled property disputes among members of the same family for their mutual benefit.
The agreements were incorporated into the final court decree.
The only property mentioned in the agreements that was outside the pending suits was covered by a clause that clarified an earlier deal and did not change legal rights in that property.
issues.conclusion: The agreements and decree were not invalid for want of registration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908 generally requires registration of instruments that create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish rights in immovable property. Section 17(2)(i) excepts composition deeds, and Section 17(2)(vi) excepts decrees or orders of a court. The court also applied the principle that family arrangements should be upheld rather than disturbed on technical or trivial grounds, particularly where the parties have received benefits under them. The clause concerning the property outside the suits merely recited existing rights and did not create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish rights in that property.

rule.if: family_composition_deed and settlement_for_mutual_family_benefit and decree_incorporates_settlement and outside_property_clause_only_recites_existing_rights

predicates.family_composition_deed: Family members enter into a written composition deed to settle their property disputes.
predicates.settlement_for_mutual_family_benefit: The arrangement is made for the mutual benefit of the participating family members.
predicates.decree_incorporates_settlement: The court incorporates the settlement into its decree.
predicates.outside_property_clause_only_recites_exi: A clause concerning property outside the pending suits merely clarifies an earlier transaction without changing rights in that property.

issues.definition: A family composition for mutual benefit, incorporated into a court decree, does not require registration when any clause concerning outside property only records existing rights.

issues.legal_issue: An assignee of a party’s interest during a pending suit is not required to seek leave to come on record, and the absence of such leave does not invalidate a settlement that ends the suit as to the assigned interest.
material_facts: The appellants had assigned their rights and liabilities in the disputed properties to the other party under their agreements.
The appellants knew of the assignments but did not seek to have them recorded in the pending suits.
The suits were being brought to an end as to the appellants’ interests rather than being continued by the assignee.
issues.conclusion: The assignee’s failure to obtain leave under Order XXII Rule 10 did not invalidate the compromise or establish an ulterior motive to defraud the appellants.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXII Rule 10 gives an assignee of an interest during a suit the option to apply for leave to continue the suit; it does not impose an obligation on the assignee to come on record. The assignor may also seek leave. Dhurandhar Prasad Singh v. Jai Prakash University, (2001) 6 SCC 534, supports the proposition that either the assignee or assignor may seek leave.

predicates.pending_suit_with_assignment: A party assigns an interest while a suit concerning that interest is pending.
predicates.assignee_does_not_seek_leave: The assignee does not apply to be brought on record or to continue the suit.
predicates.suit_ends_as_to_assigned_interest: The settlement brings the suit to an end as to the assigned interest rather than requiring the assignee to continue it.

issues.definition: When an assignee does not seek leave in a pending suit that is being settled as to the assigned interest, the absence of leave does not invalidate the settlement.

issues.legal_issue: Insufficient allegations of fraud and a mere failure to pay amounts due under a compromise decree do not justify setting the decree aside.
material_facts: The applications to set aside the decree alleged fraud but did not adequately plead the particulars supporting that allegation.
The principal complaint was that the other party had failed to pay amounts promised under the agreements.
The decree provided a means to enforce the amounts due, and the applicants had sought payment rather than initially treating non-payment as grounds to undo the settlement.
issues.conclusion: The allegations did not justify setting aside the decree; the applicants could execute it to recover the amounts due.
issues.legal_principle: A decree cannot be set aside on a fraud allegation that is inadequately pleaded. Non-payment of an amount due under a compromise decree is not, by itself, a ground to set the decree aside where the amount can be recovered by executing the decree.

rule.if: application_to_set_aside_compromise_decree and fraud_particulars_inadequate and main_ground_is_nonpayment and decree_enforceable_for_amount_due

predicates.application_to_set_aside_compromise_decr: A party applies to set aside a decree disposing of a suit by compromise.
predicates.fraud_particulars_inadequate: The application alleges fraud without adequately stating the particulars that support the allegation.
predicates.main_ground_is_nonpayment: The principal factual basis for the application is the other party’s failure to pay sums promised in the settlement.
predicates.decree_enforceable_for_amount_due: The decree can be executed to recover the amount that remains unpaid.

issues.definition: An inadequately particularized fraud allegation and an enforceable payment default do not warrant setting aside a compromise decree.
